title: In 1984, NASA crashed a remote-controlled airliner on purpose to study survival

cover.alt: A four-engine Boeing 720 airliner, tilted to one side, hitting a desert lakebed in a cloud of dust.

body: In the **Controlled Impact Demonstration**, NASA and the US Federal Aviation Administration flew an old Boeing 720 by remote control into the Mojave Desert on 1 December 1984, with crash dummies in the seats. Its tanks held about 34 tonnes of *antimisting kerosene*, jet fuel with a polymer added so that it would not spray into a fireball in a crash. The plane hit the ground askew, a steel post sliced into an engine and the fuselage, and it burned for more than an hour. The fuel failed the test, but the crash data led to new FAA rules for fire-blocking seat cushions and better-fastened floor lighting.

slides.alt: From four camera positions, a remote-controlled Boeing 720 descends over a desert lakebed, slides along the ground, breaks apart and is engulfed in a huge orange fireball.
slides.caption: 1 December 1984, Rogers Dry Lake, California: the uncrewed Boeing 720 hits the lakebed, slides, breaks up and bursts into a huge fireball.
slides.credit: NASA Dryden Flight Research Center · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: Fuel that shouldn't mist
slides.text: In a crash, fuel from torn tanks sprays out as a fine mist that ignites easily. A long-chain polymer called FM-9 thickens kerosene so it stays in drops. Engines can't burn it like that, so each of the 720's four engines had a 'degrader' that turned the fuel back into near-normal jet fuel.

slides.prompt: The plane was meant to land wings level with its engines idling. What actually happened?
slides.answer: Left wing low, nose askew, at full throttle
slides.detail: A steel wing cutter sliced into a running engine, which lit the fuel. A cutter also split the fuselage, and burning fuel got into the cabin.

slides.heading: About 1 in 4 people on board could have survived, the FAA estimated
slides.note: Estimate for a full load of 113 people: 23–25%

slides.heading: What investigators found
items: Seat cushions need fire-blocking layers, now a rule
Glued-on floor lights came loose; now they are fastened
Flight recorders sampled some data too slowly

slides.question: What was the main thing the 1984 crash was meant to test?
options: A fuel that resists catching fire
slides.explanation: The plane flew on antimisting kerosene, meant to stop a crash fireball. It didn't stop the fire, but the data led to safer seat cushions and lighting.
